caseNote: 가상 사례 (3인 배관업체 사장, 300명 규모 가구 제조사 재무팀) · 모든 인물과 수치는 설명용
insight: 회사도 '회계 소프트웨어'를 사는 게 아니라 돈을 제때 받고, 월말 결산을 빨리 끝내는 '진전'을 산다. 같은 제품도 고객마다 맡기는 일과 아픈 곳이 다르다.
misconception: 기업용 소프트웨어는 기능이 많고 리포트가 풍부할수록 잘 팔린다.

sources.text: Christensen, C. et al. (2016). Competing Against Luck. Harper Business. (Jobs to be done)
Osterwalder, A. et al. (2014). Value Proposition Design. Wiley. (Customer pains and gains)
모든 인물과 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Dana의 배관업체, 가구 제조사 재무팀, 결산 12일→5일 목표는 모두 설명용 가상 설정입니다. 실제 통계처럼 읽히지 않는지 확인하세요.
3·4번 카드의 jobs to be done, pains and gains 정의가 CUS-01-02, CUS-01-04 개념 레슨의 정의 문구와 어긋나지 않는지 확인하세요.
7번 카드의 전환 비용 언급은 CUS-02-06(고객 쪽 전환 비용)과 겹치지 않도록 한 문장 수준으로만 두었습니다.

cards.title: Nobody wants accounting software.
body: It's 10 p.m. on a Sunday. Dana runs a three-person plumbing business. She's at the kitchen table with a shoebox of receipts and a list of customers who still owe her money.
She will pay for accounting software this month. Not because she wants to do accounting. She wants this Sunday to stop happening.

image.label: A tired business owner at a kitchen table with a shoebox of receipts
image.brief: 밤 10시 부엌 식탁. 작업복 차림의 여성 배관업체 사장이 영수증이 넘치는 신발 상자와 노트북 앞에서 지친 표정. 벽시계는 10시, 창밖은 어두움. 따뜻하지만 피곤한 조명. 실제 소프트웨어 화면이나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What will make Dana pay?
body: Dana is on day 10 of a free trial of your accounting app. Which feature is most likely to turn her into a paying customer?

options.feedback: Reports look impressive in a demo, but Dana will rarely open them. They add screens without touching the work she dreads.

options.text: Send an invoice from her phone at the job, with a pay-now link
options.feedback: This does the **job she's hiring the software for**: getting paid without chasing. She'll see the result in her bank account within days.

options.text: A lower monthly price than rivals
options.feedback: Price matters to a small business. But a cheap tool that doesn't change her Sunday nights still isn't worth keeping.

cards.eyebrow: Concept at work · Jobs to be done
cards.title: She's hiring it to get paid.
body: **Jobs to be done** asks what progress a customer is trying to make when they "hire" a product. Dana's job isn't "keep the books." It's *get paid on time, stay out of trouble at tax time, and get my evenings back*.
That changes what you build and what you say. "Invoice from the van, paid by Friday" speaks to her job. "Full double-entry ledger" doesn't.
cards.softwareNote: Seen this way, your real rival isn't only other accounting apps. It's the shoebox, a spreadsheet, and the cousin who does her books once a year.

cards.eyebrow: Concept at work · Pains and gains
cards.title: Map what hurts and what she hopes for.
body: Pains are the frustrations and risks around the job. Gains are the outcomes she'd be glad to get. For Dana:
list: **Pain:** fear of a letter from the tax office
**Gain:** seeing her cash balance at a glance
**Gain:** deciding with confidence whether she can afford a second van
cards.callout: The features that sell remove a big pain or create a gain she can feel this week.
cards.softwareNote: Write your onboarding around the first pain removed. Getting a new user to send one paid invoice beats a tour of every menu.

cards.title: Inside a 300-person company, the job changes.
body: Now picture the finance team at a furniture maker. They already have accounting software. Closing each month takes 12 days of spreadsheets, and the head of finance wants it done in five.
Their pains: numbers that don't match between factories, late nights at month-end, tense weeks before the audit. Their gain: giving managers numbers they trust, sooner.
Same product category. A completely different job.

image.label: Two scenes side by side: a plumber's van and a finance office at month-end
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽: 배관 작업 현장 밴 앞에서 휴대폰으로 청구서를 보내는 사장, 말풍선 "Get paid". 오른쪽: 사무실에서 서류와 모니터에 둘러싸인 재무팀, 달력에 월말 표시, 말풍선 "Close faster". 가운데에 같은 노트북 아이콘. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: You're asked to pick the new system.
body: You're a finance manager at the furniture maker. Your boss asks you to compare three accounting systems and recommend one.

options.text: Build a spreadsheet comparing every feature of all three
options.feedback: Thorough, but every system ticks most boxes. Without knowing which pains cost you most, the longest feature list tends to win.

options.text: List the team's biggest pains, like the 12-day close, and test each system on those
options.feedback: This puts **pains and gains** to work. You judge each system by whether it shortens the close and fixes mismatched numbers, not by its brochure.

options.text: Pick what similar companies in your industry use
options.feedback: It lowers the risk of a bad pick, and peers make good references. But their job may not be yours, so check it against your own pains.

cards.title: What people ask for isn't always the job.
body: Customers often name a feature when they mean a pain. "We need better reports" may really mean "the boss keeps asking for numbers and we can't answer fast."
Change itself is a pain, too. Moving years of records, retraining staff and risking errors at month-end are real costs. A new tool must beat the old one by enough to cover them.
So look at what people struggle with, not only what they request.

cards.title: Companies buy progress, not software.
body: **Concepts used:** *jobs to be done* (Dana hires software to get paid; the finance team hires it to close faster) and *pains and gains* (judging any tool by the pains it removes and the gains it creates).
**Try it today:** pick one tool your business pays for. Write down the job you hired it for and the biggest pain it removed. If you can't name either, question the bill.
